I'm reading this from the image alone, and some of the text is cut off or overlaps.

1. The animation seems to show how inflation affects the buying power of a payment that stays the same. The chart is US consumer prices (CPI-U) from Aug 2006 to Aug 2026. It is labeled "illustrative" and "US only · history, not a forecast." It has two checks. A "first check" is a flat line, and a "level check" is a line that falls away from it.

2. In frames 1 to 2, a line is drawn from left to right. The dots that track the first check stay near the flat reference line. They dip slightly at the start and the end. The level-check line drifts steadily downward and ends well below the flat line. In frame 3, a dashed marker appears at year 5 with the label "level check: about 9 in 10 by year 5." In frame 4, a "rising check: there after 20 years" label appears, and part of it is unreadable because it overlaps the "first check" label. In frames 5 and 6, a "?" appears at the top right.

3. My reading is that a payment fixed at today's amount (the flat "first check") buys less as prices rise. By year 5 it buys only about 90% of what it did at the start, and the loss keeps growing over 20 years. The "rising check" seems to be a payment that increases over time, but I can't tell how it is meant to compare. The "?" suggests the outcome is uncertain, and the caption says the past isn't a forecast.

4. The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer might take away that inflation erodes a fixed payment over a long retirement. They might also take away that it's worth asking whether a payout option rises over time. That is the point I'd relate to your two annuity options. The animation doesn't say which option to pick.

5. That takeaway is my own conclusion, not something the animation states. It only shows the pattern and the "history, not a forecast" caveat.
